new_statements.quote: 1.2.6 All junctures share two characteristics: there is a potential for silence, and the first vowel following any juncture is more strongly stressed than others, in relatively slow speech. In the most rapidly spoken utterances observed, the stress differences were leveled, along with the disappearance of all pauses between words. This allows for a phonological definition of a word in Thargari: a segment bounded by a juncture and itself containing no juncture. The forms isolated in this way correspond to the word as defined in 3.1 Word structure. Word juncture has only the minimal features of a juncture as outlined above. A word in an utterance is considered to be bounded by this juncture.

In the most rapidly spoken utterances observed, the stress differences were leveled, along with the disappearance of all pauses between words. new_statements.rule_in_words: Stress is non-contrastive and falls on the first vowel (first syllable) of every phonological word; Klokeid uses this post-juncture initial stress as the criterion delimiting the word. In fast speech the stress differences level out.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Nothing said about secondary or rhythmic stress.
new_statements.exceptions: None; only the remark that in the most rapid speech stress differences are leveled and inter-word pauses disappear.
new_statements.domain_note: Phonological word (root plus suffixes/enclitics, = the unit bounded by word juncture); statement framed via junctures in connected utterances, based on 1967 Carnarvon fieldwork (c. 1500 sentences, 1000+ isolated words, tapes). Describes the l-dialect of Thargari (speakers Tommy Dodd, Donald, Chubby Yowadji); a 'd-dialect' is mentioned as phonologically different.
new_statements.identity_note: Klokeid 1969 describes 'Thargari' (= Tharrkari/Dhargari, dhar1247, ISO dhr), specifically the l-dialect spoken by three Carnarvon-area men in 1967; he notes a phonologically divergent 'd-dialect'. Current Wikipedia/Austin usage treats Tharrkari as one of the Mantharta languages (with Jiwarli, Warriyangka, Thiin); the statement applies to dhar1247 proper.

I.e. word-initial stress, used to define the phonological word. No statement on secondary stress.
